```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
data(penguins)
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep))
# typst-render: register the passthrough knitr engine so {typst} blocks reach the filter
source(file.path(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR"),
                 "_extensions/mcanouil/typst-render/_resources/typst_define.R"))
```

## Learning Outcomes

After this session you will be able to:

- author a Quarto document natively (`.qmd`), with figures, tables, cross-references, and math;
- lay a document out — the article grid, and content in the margin;
- make it **accessible** — alt text, color-blind-safe colors, a built-in contrast check;
- turn it into a **cited, branded Typst PDF** — no LaTeX.

By the end: one penguins document carried all the way to a **polished, citable PDF**.

::: notes
- **Frame:** you already write R and have met R Markdown or Quarto — today is about what Quarto
  *adds* and how far one `.qmd` can go, not "what is a code chunk". We build one document and
  carry it all the way to a citable, branded PDF.
:::

# Part 1 — Basics {.center}

Author a document, land it as HTML.

## What you can now build {#what-quarto-is}

You know the literate-programming idea. In 2026, one `.qmd` is your source for:

::: {.incremental}
- a **report** (HTML, PDF, Word) — figures, tables, cross-refs, citations;
- a **presentation** (these slides are a `.qmd`);
- a **website or book** (Day 2) — many pages, one config;
- a **branded PDF via Typst** *(a modern PDF engine bundled in Quarto, no LaTeX)* — a publication-ready article.
:::

. . .

One tool, many outputs, multiple languages: **all from one plain-text `.qmd` you write directly.**

::: notes
- **Frame (not a line):** reframe from "Quarto = R Markdown++, nothing new to learn" to "here's
  what you can now build" — this audience wants to go further, not be reassured.
:::

## How it all works {#how-it-works}

`quarto render report.qmd` runs your code, then hands Markdown to Pandoc:

```{typst}
#| echo: false
//| align: center
//| alt: "Flowchart: .qmd, .ipynb and .md files each go through an engine (knitr, Jupyter, or Markdown) to Pandoc, which renders HTML, PDF, and Word or PowerPoint outputs."
#import "@preview/fletcher:0.5.8" as fletcher: diagram, node, edge

#let teal = rgb("#4C979F")
#let fill = rgb("#D1E5E6")
#let ink = rgb("#1c2833")
#set text(font: ("Albert Sans", "DejaVu Sans"), size: 16pt, fill: ink)

#diagram(
  spacing: (16mm, 8mm),
  node-stroke: teal + 0.8pt,
  node-fill: fill,
  node-inset: 8pt,
  node-corner-radius: 4pt,
  edge-stroke: teal + 0.9pt,

  // inputs
  node((0, 0), [`.qmd` \ text + code], name: <qmd>),
  node((0, 1), [`.ipynb` \ Jupyter], name: <ipynb>),
  node((0, 2), [`.md` \ text only], name: <md>),
  // engines
  node((1, 0), [knitr engine \ R · Python · Julia], name: <knitr>, corner-radius: 20pt),
  node((1, 1), [Jupyter engine], name: <jup>, corner-radius: 20pt),
  node((1, 2), [Markdown engine], name: <mde>, corner-radius: 20pt),
  // pandoc
  node((2, 1), text(fill: white)[*Pandoc*], name: <pandoc>, corner-radius: 20pt, fill: teal),
  // outputs
  node((3, 0), [HTML \ reports · sites · slides], name: <html>),
  node((3, 1), [PDF \ Typst or LaTeX], name: <pdf>),
  node((3, 2), [Word · PowerPoint], name: <office>),

  edge(<qmd>, <knitr>, "->"),
  edge(<ipynb>, <jup>, "->"),
  edge(<md>, <mde>, "->"),
  edge(<knitr>, <pandoc>, "->"),
  edge(<jup>, <pandoc>, "->"),
  edge(<mde>, <pandoc>, "->"),
  edge(<pandoc>, <html>, "->"),
  edge(<pandoc>, <pdf>, "->"),
  edge(<pandoc>, <office>, "->"),
)
```

::: notes
- **Frame:** for R, the **knitr** engine runs your chunks — the same engine as R Markdown. Your
  `.Rmd` still renders as-is; `knitr::convert_chunk_header()` moves it to `.qmd` cell options when
  you're ready.
:::

## Anatomy of a `.qmd` {#anatomy}

Three parts: a YAML header, Markdown prose, and executable code cells.

```` {.markdown code-line-numbers="|1-4|6|8-13"}
---
title: "A penguin story"
format: html
---

We measured **`{{r}} nrow(penguins)`** penguins.

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-bill
#| fig-cap: "Bill length versus depth"
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep, color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```
````

. . .

Cell options use the `#|` "hash-pipe": one option per line, YAML-valued. Native from the start.

## Markdown & content — think in deltas {#markdown-content}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
In `day1-intro/`, create **`my-report.qmd`** with `format: html`. It is the file the lab starts from.
Put this cell at the top: everything we write next assumes it. Fallen behind at any point? Open
`starter.qmd` in the same folder and keep going from there.
:::

```` {.markdown}
```{{r}}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
data(penguins)
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep))
```
````

You already know Markdown. Quarto adds the research-writing pieces: **figures** and **tables** with
captions, **cross-references** (`@fig-bill`, `@tbl-summary`, `@eq-ratio`), **math**, **inline code**
that reports numbers from the data, and **callouts**.

::: notes
- **Say:** "From here we build one document together. Render as we go."
- **Do:** make sure the setup cell is **in the document**, not run in the console. knitr renders in a fresh R process, so a console run never reaches the render and the first figure cell errors.
- **Say (name the file out loud):** "`my-report.qmd`, in `day1-intro/`" — it is the exact file the Authoring Challenge asks for, so what they build now carries straight into the lab.
- **Frame:** the list is *deltas* over the Markdown they already know — not a Markdown lesson.
- **Timing:** this + the next four slides (Figures / Tables & math / Callouts / Inline code) are the live build, ~8–10 min total. One point per slide; don't polish plots.
:::

## Figures & cross-references {#figures}

A labeled code cell becomes a numbered, referenceable figure:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| label: fig-bill
#| fig-cap: "Bill length versus depth, by species."
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Scatter plot of bill depth against bill length
#|   for three penguin species, forming clusters.
#| output-location: column
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)",
       y = "Bill depth (mm)")
```

Refer to it in prose with `@fig-bill` → renders as "@fig-bill", a live link. Labels must start
with `fig-` / `tbl-` / `eq-` to be cross-referenceable.

`#| fig-alt` is the figure's alt text (the description screen readers announce). Add it to every
figure. (`#| output-location: column` is **slide-only**: a revealjs placement, not article layout.)

::: notes
- **Do:** add `#| label: fig-bill` + `#| fig-cap` to the plot cell, render, show the auto-number appear.
- **Say:** "A labeled cell *becomes* a numbered figure; `@fig-bill` in prose is a live link."
- **Say (trap):** the label must start `fig-`/`tbl-`/`eq-`, or the ref renders a stray `?@`.
- **Do:** point at `output-location: column` — a revealjs cell option that puts the plot in a column *beside the code on this slide*. (Presentation output-placement — **not** the article margin layout on the Layouts slide, which doesn't apply to revealjs.)
:::

## Tables {#tables}

`gt` (or `knitr::kable`) turns a data frame into a table; a `#| label: tbl-` makes it referenceable.

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mean bill length per species."
penguins |>
  summarise(bill = mean(bill_len), .by = species) |>
  gt() |> fmt_number(bill, decimals = 1)
```

Then refer to it in prose with `@tbl-summary` (same mechanic as figures).

::: notes
- **Do:** show the `gt` cell with `#| label: tbl-summary`, render, point at the auto-number.
- **Say:** "Same mechanic as figures — a `tbl-` label makes it referenceable; `gt` or `knitr::kable`, your call."
- **Timing:** the table is the must-keep; the Math slide is the trim point if Part 1 is tight.
:::

## Math {#math}

Display math with a label is cross-referenceable too:

``` markdown
$$
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill\_len}}{\text{bill\_dep}}
$$ {#eq-ratio}
```

renders as @eq-ratio below:

$$
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill\_len}}{\text{bill\_dep}}
$$ {#eq-ratio}

::: notes
- **Do:** show the display-math block with `{#eq-ratio}`, then the rendered, numbered equation.
- **Say:** "Same mechanic again — an `eq-` label makes the equation referenceable."
- **Say (trap):** inside bare `$$…$$` an underscore can trigger a subscript (or an error) depending on the math renderer — escape it as `bill\_len` (the lab warns about this too).
:::

## Callouts {#callouts}

Callouts are first-class Markdown (no package):

``` markdown
::: {.callout-tip}
Base-R `penguins` (R ≥ 4.5) needs no install.
:::
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Base-R `penguins` (R ≥ 4.5) needs no install.
:::

::: notes
- **Do:** render one callout live — no package, pure Markdown.
- **Say:** "Five types — note, tip, warning, caution, important — same syntax, different color."
- **Frame:** next slide closes the live build — inline code.
:::

## Inline code {#inline-code}

**Inline code** drops a computed value straight into prose. Put it in a sentence:

``` markdown
We measured `{{r}} nrow(penguins)` penguins.
```

. . .

It renders with the live count: "We measured **`{r} nrow(penguins)`** penguins."

. . .

The number updates when the data does. **Reproducible by construction.**

::: notes
- **Do:** show inline code reporting `nrow(penguins)` from the data — "the number updates when the data does. Reproducible by construction."
- Closes the live build — next we step back to layout.
:::

## Layouts: body, margin, and beyond {#layouts}

::: {.callout-warning title="Eyes up — not a live *Follow along*"}
The live build is done. The next seven slides are concept, no need to type along. Your document is
ready for the Challenge.
:::

The **article-layout model** puts content in the **body**, the **margin**, or a zone **wider than
the body** (in the paged formats: HTML, LaTeX, Typst):

- `page-layout: article` / `full` — the overall grid;
- **margin** content — figures, tables, captions, `.aside`, footnotes;
- **outset / inset** — a figure or table that spills *beyond* the body (outset) or widens toward
  the page while keeping a margin from the edge (inset);
- **multi-column** `::: {.columns}` and **panels** — tabsets + `layout-ncol`.

::: notes
- **Do:** gloss outset/inset on first use; the rendered visual examples live behind the **Learn
  more** links on the next slide, for anyone who wants the full column vocabulary.
:::

## Put output in the margin {#margin-layout}

A cell's `#| column: margin` drops its output (figure or table, caption and all) into the margin:

```` {.markdown}
```{{r}}
#| label: counts
#| column: margin
penguins |> count(species, name = "n") |> knitr::kable()
```
````

*In the lab you'll use **margin** layout, the one that does the most for an article. The rest are
in the Quarto docs below.*

**Learn more:** [Article Layout](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/article-layout.html) ·
[Margin content](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/article-layout.html#margin-content)

::: notes
- **Say:** "Margin figures still take `@fig-`/`@tbl-` — so layout pairs naturally with cross-refs."
:::

## Make it accessible {#accessibility}

Accessibility is a few habits layered on what you already write:

- **Alt text** — you already add `#| fig-alt:` to every figure; it's what a screen reader announces.
- **Color-blind-safe colors** — the default palette isn't. Reach for **Okabe-Ito**
  (`scale_color_okabe_ito()`) or **viridis**, and encode by shape/label too, not color alone.
- **Check contrast** — WCAG wants 4.5:1 on text. Quarto's built-in `axe` runs axe-core on the
  rendered page: `axe: true` logs to dev-tools, `axe: {output: document}` writes the report onto the
  page itself.

**Learn more:** [HTML Accessibility](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-accessibility.html)

::: notes
- **Hook:** your reader might be on a projector in a bright room, have red-green color-vision
  deficiency (~8% of men), or use a screen reader — the same few habits cover all three.
- **Tie to their plot:** the penguins scatter defaults to non-safe colors; one line,
  `scale_color_okabe_ito()`, fixes it (the worked report already uses it) — show before/after if time.
- **`axe`:** it's axe-core (the industry-standard checker), built into Quarto since 1.8 for
  html/revealjs/dashboard; it runs in the browser on **preview** and logs to dev-tools — a
  check-as-you-go tool, not a render/publish gate. Quarto 1.10 polishes the on-page report.
:::

## One source → many formats {#document-types}

One key in the header picks the output. The content stays put:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.yaml code-line-numbers="false"}
format: [html, typst]     # render several at once
toc: true                 # shared — applies to both
```

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="false"}
format:                   # …or set options per format
  html:
    toc: false
  typst:
    toc: true
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Shared vs. per-format** — top-level keys (`toc`, `number-sections`, …) apply to every format; the `format:` map overrides them per output.
- **Conditional content** — show or hide per format with
  `::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}`.
- The *layout* idioms adapt per format: write once, target many.
:::
::::

**Learn more:** [Multiple formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-multi-format.html) ·
[Conditional content](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/conditional.html)

## Execution: set once, override per cell {#execution}

R Markdown's `knitr::opts_chunk$set()` moves into the header. Set defaults once, override per cell:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Header — defaults for every cell:

``` yaml
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
A cell — overrides locally with `#|`:

```` {.markdown}
```{{r}}
#| echo: true
summary(penguins$body_mass)
```
````
:::
::::

The header sets the defaults; a cell's `#|` wins.

*`freeze` commits computed results to `_freeze/` so a project re-render (or CI without R) skips
unchanged documents. That's the Day 2 story.*

**Learn more:** [Execution options](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html) ·
[Cell options](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-knitr.html)

::: notes
- **Do (live):** add `execute:` / `echo: false` to the header, re-render — every code block
  disappears at once. Then drop `#| echo: true` on one cell — just that one returns. The delta,
  made visible.
- **Say:** "Same idea as `opts_chunk$set()`, now declarative YAML — dashes not dots, `false` not
  `FALSE`."
- `freeze` is a one-line teaser only; the real freeze-vs-cache teach is Day 2.
:::

## Running & editing {#running}

Drive Quarto from the CLI, in whatever editor you like:

``` bash
quarto preview report.qmd   # live-reloading preview
quarto render  report.qmd   # one-off render
```

- **RStudio**, **Positron**, and **VS Code** all work. The **visual editor** (WYSIWYM — *what you
  see is what you mean*) is built into the **RStudio IDE**, and comes to **Positron and VS Code**
  through the **Quarto extension**.
- The same `quarto render` also takes **`-P name:value`**: override a document *parameter* to get
  one report per sample or species from a single source. *(Optional bonus in today's lab.)*

::: notes
- **Do:** run `quarto preview report.qmd` live — save an edit, show the browser reload; then
  `quarto render` for the one-off.
- **Say:** "Drive it from the CLI, in whatever editor you like — RStudio, Positron, VS Code."
- **Params (MENTION, cut-first):** mention `-P` here, where `quarto render` is on screen — the
  optional lab bonus does it hands-on (one report per species). Don't dwell; it isn't a taught beat.
- **Timing:** keep it brief — the room knows cells and Jenny Bryan covers the IDE. Part 1 lands

:::

## From report to article {#report-to-article}

You have a clean HTML document. The lab ships a **Part-2 starter** if you need one. To make it a
**publication-ready article**, two more things:

::: {.incremental}
1. **citations** — a `.bib` file and a citation style;
2. **a typeset PDF** — via **Typst**, bundled in Quarto.
:::

. . .

This is exactly the path from your analysis to a submission, and to your **team-project** write-up.

## Citations {#citations}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
Back in your editor: we add citations to your Part-1 document, or to `day1-intro/starter.qmd` if you
need one.
:::

Point the header at a `.bib`, then cite with `@key`:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
``` yaml
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
```
``` markdown
The data come from Palmer Station
[@gorman2014].
```
renders as: … Palmer Station (Gorman et al., 2014).
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
`references.bib` already ships in `day1-intro/` (excerpt):

``` {.bibtex}
@article{gorman2014,
  author  = {Gorman, K. B. and ...},
  title   = {Ecological Sexual ...},
  journal = {PLoS ONE},
  year    = {2014}
}
```
:::
::::

The reference list renders at the end automatically, or wherever you drop this div:

``` markdown
::: {#refs}
:::
```

**CSL** = *Citation Style Language*. Swap the `csl:` file to restyle every citation.

::: notes
- **Do:** point the header at `references.bib` + a `csl:`, drop `[@gorman2014]` into a sentence,
  re-render — the in-text cite resolves and a reference list appears at the end.
- **Say:** "One `.bib` key in your prose becomes a formatted citation *and* an auto-built reference
  list — swap the `csl:` file and the whole style changes."
- **Gloss CSL if asked:** *Citation Style Language* — the file that decides how citations and the
  reference list are formatted (APA, Vancouver, a journal's own style).
- **Helpers:** the `.bib` path is relative to the document — the follow-along file must sit in
  `day1-intro/` next to `references.bib`/`apa.csl`. A `[?]` in the text means a wrong `@key`, or
  `bibliography:` not set in the header.
:::

## A real title block {#authors}

A few header lines turn the document into a publication-ready article (name, affiliation, ORCID, abstract):

``` yaml
title: "Bill shape distinguishes Antarctic penguins"
author:
  - name: Christophe Dervieux
    affiliation: Posit, PBC
    email: cderv@posit.co
    orcid: 0000-0003-4474-2498
abstract: |
  Using base-R `penguins`, we show bill shape separates species...
```

Renders in HTML, PDF, and Typst. Write it once.

::: notes
- **Timing (Part-2 trim-first):** if Part 2 runs long, this is the slide to cut — name author / affiliation / ORCID / abstract verbally and move on. Citations, Typst, and brand are the must-keeps.
:::

## Typst — modern PDF, no LaTeX {#typst}

**Typst** is a modern typesetting system that **ships inside Quarto**: nothing to install, no
LaTeX toolchain.

``` yaml
format: typst
```

That is the whole switch. Then re-render:

``` bash
quarto render report.qmd --to typst
```

::: {.callout-note title="Pre-flight"}
Typst is bundled from Quarto **1.4+**; we require **≥ 1.9** (margin/article layout). Check once with `quarto --version`.
:::

::: notes
- **Say:** "Typst is deterministic and bundled — nothing to install. LaTeX is still there if you
  need it, but Typst is what we use in 2026."
- Gloss "Typst" on first use.
- **If someone says their PDF is serif despite `_brand.yml` (only if asked):** check for
  `unknown font family: albert sans` in the log. That is a font *download* failure (no network on
  the first render), not a missing brand file. Colors and layout are still branded.
:::

## Branding the PDF — `_brand.yml` {#brand}

One `_brand.yml` carries your palette + fonts to the **Typst PDF** you just built, and to the
**plots and tables** inside it:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
``` {.yaml filename="_brand.yml"}
color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Same file themes HTML and Typst.
- The R side (`theme_brand_ggplot2()` / `theme_brand_gt()` from the **brand.yml** package) themes
  your **plots and tables** from the *same* palette.
- Quarto fetches Google fonts for Typst automatically.
:::
::::

::: notes
- **Do:** add `_brand.yml` (palette + fonts) and re-render the Typst PDF — colors and type change
  from that one file. This is the payoff.
- **Say:** "One file themes the **PDF** — and `theme_brand_ggplot2()` / `_gt()` pull the *same*
  palette into your plots and tables. Tomorrow the *same* file will brand a whole project."
- **Helpers:** a plot won't inherit the palette until you add a `theme_brand_*` helper; the first
  Typst render fetches the Google fonts, so it needs network once.
:::

::: notes
- **Say (handoff):** "Last part — Citations Challenge: add a `.bib`, render a branded Typst PDF, and you leave with a publication-ready article — a branded, citable PDF. ~30 min; helpers are around."
- **Helpers:** the `.bib` key must match `@key` exactly; the Typst Google-font fetch needs network on the first render; a missing `csl:` falls back to Typst's native style. "Where's my PDF?" — in `day1-intro/` it lands next to its source (`starter.qmd` → `starter.pdf`, `my-report.qmd` → `my-report.pdf`), no `_site/` redirect. All covered by the lab's hint/solution.
:::

## What you can do now {#wrap-up}

You can now:

- author a `.qmd` natively — figures, tables, cross-references, math, callouts;
- lay it out — the article grid, and content in the margin;
- make it accessible — alt text, color-blind-safe colors, a built-in `axe` check;
- cite it with a `.bib` + CSL, give it a real title block;
- ship it as a **branded Typst PDF** — no LaTeX.

. . .

**Next (Day 2):** grow one document into a whole **project**, a website your team can publish.
